'''T. Don Tilley''' (born in [[Norman, Oklahoma]], November 22, 1954) is a professor of chemistry at the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.cchem.berkeley.edu/tdtgroup/groupmembers/tdtilley.html|title=T. Don Tilley|website=www.cchem.berkeley.edu|access-date=2017-07-07}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/tilley|title=T. Don Tilley {{!}} College of Chemistry|website=chemistry.berkeley.edu|access-date=2017-07-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Waterman|first=Rory|date=2014-10-01|title=Editorial|journal=Inorganica Chimica Acta|series=Special issue: Dedicated to Don Tilley|volume=422|pages=1–2|doi=10.1016/j.ica.2014.07.048}}</ref>

__TOC__

== Career ==
In 1977, Tilley received his B.S. degree in chemistry from the [[University of Texas at Austin|University of Texas]].<ref name=":0" /> In 1982, he earned his Ph.D. degree from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] for his research on [[organolanthanide chemistry]] with Professor Richard A. Andersen.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tilley|first1=T. Don|last2=Andersen|first2=Richard A.|last3=Zalkin|first3=Allan|date=1982-06-01|title=Tertiary phosphine complexes of the f-block metals. Crystal structure of Yb[N(SiMe3)2]2[Me2PCH2CH2PMe2]: evidence for a ytterbium-.gamma.-carbon interaction|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|volume=104|issue=13|pages=3725–3727|doi=10.1021/ja00377a033|bibcode=1982JAChS.104.3725T |issn=0002-7863}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tilley|first1=T. Don.|last2=Andersen|first2=Richard A.|date=1981-10-01|title=Pentamethylcyclopentadienyl derivatives of the trivalent lanthanide elements neodymium, samarium, and ytterbium|journal=Inorganic Chemistry|volume=20|issue=10|pages=3267–3270|doi=10.1021/ic50224a025|s2cid=55083879 |issn=0020-1669|url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc839331/}}</ref>

Afterwards, he conducted post-doctoral research with [[Robert H. Grubbs|Prof. Robert H. Grubbs]] and [[John E. Bercaw|Prof. John E. Bercaw]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]] and with Luigi Venanzi and Piero Pino at [[ETH Zurich|ETH]] in Switzerland, during which he developed the chemistry of the (pentamethylcyclopentadienyl)ruthenium fragment ([Cp*Ru]).<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Tilley|first1=T. Don|last2=Grubbs|first2=Robert H.|last3=Bercaw|first3=John E.|date=1984-02-01|title=Halide, hydride, and alkyl derivatives of (pentamethylcyclopentadienyl)bis(trimethylphosphine)ruthenium|journal=Organometallics|volume=3|issue=2|pages=274–278|doi=10.1021/om00080a019|issn=0276-7333}}</ref>

He started his independent research career at [[University of California, San Diego|UC San Diego]] in 1983, where he was promoted to associate professor in 1988, and to Professor in 1990. In 1994, he accepted appointments as a professor of chemistry at [[University of California, Berkeley|UC Berkeley]] and Faculty Senior Scientist at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] (LBNL).<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://commons.lbl.gov/display/csd/T.+Don+Tilley|title=T. Don Tilley - Chemical Sciences Division Chemical Sciences Division|website=commons.lbl.gov|access-date=2017-07-07}}</ref>

Throughout his career, he has published over 430 papers on various subjects in [[organometallic]] and [[inorganic chemistry]], as well as [[materials science]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cchem.berkeley.edu/tdtgroup/publications.html|title=Publications|website=www.cchem.berkeley.edu|access-date=2017-07-07}}</ref> Since 2005, Tilley has also served as the North American Associate Editor for ''[[Chemical Communications]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.rsc.org/journals-books-databases/about-journals/chemcomm/|title=Chemical Communications|last=Chemistry|first=Royal Society of|date=2015-05-22|website=www.rsc.org|language=en|access-date=2017-07-07}}</ref>

== Research ==
Tilley's research group conducts exploratory synthetic, structural, and reactivity studies of inorganic and organometallic systems. His research program includes: [[organometallic chemistry]] and [[homogenous catalysis]], materials chemistry and [[heterogenous catalysis]], organic [[electronic materials]], [[supramolecular chemistry]], and [[solar energy conversion]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cchem.berkeley.edu/tdtgroup/research.html|title=Research|website=www.cchem.berkeley.edu|access-date=2017-07-07}}</ref>
